structure.title: Preface
structure.summary: This document is a formal notice from Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited (ONGC) regarding its 32nd Annual General Meeting (AGM) scheduled for August 29, 2025, to be held via video conferencing/other audio-visual means. It informs stock exchanges (NSE and BSE) about the AGM and Integrated Annual Report for FY25, which are being sent electronically to members. The notice details the AGM business: adoption of audited financial statements, declaration of a final dividend of ₹1.25 per equity share, appointment of a retiring director, authorization of auditor remuneration, and special resolutions for appointing three directors (Arunangshu Sarkar, Vikram Saxena, and Om Prakash Sinha). It also provides remote e-voting details (from August 25 to August 28, 2025), cut-off date (August 22, 2025), record date for dividend (September 4, 2025), and contact information of the Company Secretary.

The text also includes the company's CIN and registered office details.

nodes.title: ONGC Annual Report (intro)
nodes.summary: At ONGC, we recognize that the future demands more than just growth; it calls for responsibility. That is why we have set a clear, time-bound goal: to achieve Net Zero carbon emissions by 2038. While continuing to power the nation with conventional energy to ensure energy security, we are simultaneously accelerating our shift toward renewable energy. Our aim is clear: to fuel progress with minimal environmental impact. This decisive transformation in the energy landscape is not just our mission; it is our unwavering commitment to the nation.Climbing with Purpose - ONGC’s Spirit Never Stops

nodes.title: Board of Directors

nodes.title: STANDALONE PERFORMANCE AT A GLANCE

structure.title: ONGC Integrated Annual Report
structure.summary: The ONGC Integrated Annual Report FY 2024-25 covers financial and non-financial performance under the <IR> Framework and GRI Standards, detailing the reporting period, six capitals, scope, double materiality assessment, assurance, and feedback solicitation. It outlines the theme 'Energizing Innovation for a Self-Reliant Green India', Energy Strategy 2040, and value creation through six capitals. The report presents ONGC's vision, strategic priorities, stakeholder engagement framework, and the double materiality matrix with 16 material issues. It addresses occupational health and safety, water and waste management, economic performance, and progress targets. Value creation is detailed through manufactured, financial, natural, intellectual, and human capitals, including production highlights, discoveries, collaborations, and renewable energy expansion. Human-centric approach covers workforce strength, training, diversity, grievance redressal, and human rights. Moving forward highlights CSR expenditure, awards, and SDG impacts. Management approach to community engagement includes CSR initiatives, education, skill training, healthcare, and community development. Governance covers board diversity, risk management, sustainability governance, and GRI mapping. The report concludes with GRI index, glossary, and Board's Report on financial and operational performance.

nodes.title: Reporting Period
nodes.summary: This Integrated Report for FY 2024-25 by ONGC covers financial and non-financial performance, prepared under the <IR> Framework, GRI Standards, and applicable regulations. It details the reporting period, six capitals (financial, manufactured, human, intellectual, social, natural), and scope including parent company, key subsidiaries (OVL, MRPL, OPaL), and joint venture (OTPC), while noting broader group entities. It explains the first Double Materiality Assessment, restatement of Scope 3 emissions, independent assurance by Bureau Veritas, and a responsibility statement, summarizing all key sections and disclosures.

nodes.title: Feedback
nodes.summary: The text covers stakeholder feedback solicitation via email for the integrated annual report, a forward-looking statements disclaimer, and the report's theme 'Energizing Innovation for a Self-Reliant Green India' emphasizing ONGC's role in sustainable energy, innovation, low-carbon technologies, and alignment with Viksit Bharat and Net Zero 2070. It details Energy Strategy 2040 with targets for production, revenue, profit, renewable expansion, and investments in carbon capture and green hydrogen. It introduces a four-pronged business strategy and explains value creation through six capitals: intellectual, human, financial, manufactured, natural, and social/relationship, each with specific focus areas, all contributing to the 2038 net-zero goal.

nodes.title: Section 2: Overview of Company and Priority Management
nodes.summary: This text outlines ONGC's vision to be a global integrated energy leader through sustainable growth, R&D, ethics, safety, and customer focus. It details strategic priorities: integrated energy business, dominant Indian leadership, carbon neutrality, and stakeholder engagement. Stakeholder engagement is described as key to strategy, with a robust mechanism involving surveys and feedback. Seven stakeholder groups are identified: customers, employees, industrial associations, investors, suppliers, regulatory bodies, and communities/NGOs. Engagement objectives include assessing satisfaction, identifying improvements, and detecting risks. A four-stage process—Plan, Identify, Engage, Report—is explained. Insights are integrated into business planning via the Carbon Management and Sustainability Group and Management Committee, with FY 2024-25 focus areas: occupational health and safety, energy management, human capital management, and GHG/air emissions management.

nodes.title: Stakeholder Engagement Framework
nodes.summary: The text presents ONGC's Stakeholder Engagement Framework, detailing engagement with employees, customers, investors, regulatory bodies, communities, suppliers, and industry associations, including their expectations, engagement channels, types (information, consultation, participation), and frequency. It outlines the Double Materiality Assessment (GRI 3-1, 3-2, 3-3) conducted in FY 2024-25, covering its rationale, standards (GRI, CSRD/ESRS, EFRAG), integration with ERM, review process, and data sources. It explains the concept of double materiality (impact and financial) and details the assessment process: defining the sustainability landscape, identifying impacts/risks/opportunities, prioritizing 16 material issues, management oversight, assessment factors, methodology steps, and validation by the Management Committee. The document concludes with an assessment matrix.

nodes.title: Operations
nodes.summary: ONGC addresses water management by monitoring usage, aligning with Jal Shakti Mission, adopting efficient technologies, and investing in wastewater treatment for recycling. Economic performance risks include project delays, cost overruns, and energy market volatility, mitigated through monitoring, diversification, compliance, and green financing. Waste management tackles hazardous and non-hazardous waste from operations, ensuring regulatory compliance and transitioning to a circular economy via reuse, recycling, waste-to-energy projects, and collaborations like BARC for advanced water recycling, plus exploring waste treatment facilities. The response strategy uses a management system with KPIs to review goals and performance.

nodes.title: Target

It also addresses material issues for external stakeholders through impact valuation, and climate adaptation, resilience and mitigation for operational continuity and regulatory alignment.

nodes.title: Targets

It addresses emerging risks in low-carbon investments and ONGC's mitigation strategy through financial modeling and portfolio reviews. The document outlines the value creation model with inputs, enablers, and outputs across six capitals: financial (total income, expenses, PAT, debt-equity ratio), natural (clean energy generation, CO2 reduction), human (training, women representation, attrition), manufactured (production, discoveries, wells), intellectual (patents, copyrights, R&D expenditure), and social & relationship (CSR spend, beneficiaries, supplier base). It also highlights innovation, sustainability, governance, and alignment with national priorities.

nodes.title: Human Centric Approach
nodes.summary: The text details ONGC's human-centric approach, covering strategic human capital management with policies to attract, develop, and retain talent, emphasizing inclusivity, diversity, and equity. It reports workforce strength (29,986 employees, 91.63% male, 8.37% female, a 5.94% increase), hiring (50 employees, 14% female, 80% under 30), and engagement of 1,072 apprentices. It outlines training investments (₹4,582 million, average 27.8 hours per employee), leadership programs (Unnati Shikhar, Unnati Udhyam), digital platform Udbhav, ESG training, IT sensitization, and employee satisfaction initiatives including benefits, work-life balance, audits, and employee representation. Diversity and inclusion efforts cover equal opportunity policy, women in leadership, and persons with disabilities (over 2% of workforce). Grievance redressal mechanisms include a four-level system and web portal, with reported cases of sexual harassment and discrimination. Health and safety initiatives include HSE management, audits, safety culture programs, mental health support, emergency drills, and digital safety systems, with LTIFR reduced by 14.71%. Human rights commitments align with UN Global Compact and include policy implementation and grievance mechanisms.

nodes.title: Moving Forward
nodes.summary: ONGC's strategy focuses on human capital for energy security and sustainable growth, building a future-ready workforce through technology, global collaborations, and talent development, while promoting a safe, inclusive, and diverse workplace. It enhances employee engagement via open communication and feedback. The company values stakeholder relationships for long-term success and social welfare, co-creating solutions with partners, clients, regulators, NGOs, and communities. Key highlights include UN SDGs impacted, total CSR expenditure of ₹10,168.20 million in FY 2024-25, alignment with material issues, a 46% increase in CSR expenditure, the 23rd Asia Pacific HRM Congress Award 2024 for Best Use of CSR Practices, 45 aspirational districts covered, and ₹4,418.65 million spent on healthcare, hunger, and poverty eradication.

nodes.title: Management Approach
nodes.summary: ONGC's management approach to community engagement emphasizes inclusive, sustainable growth through CSR and sustainability initiatives focused on underserved communities, strengthened by local partnerships and community-led planning. The CSR & ESG Committee guides and monitors these initiatives, which span education and skill development, healthcare, community development, infrastructure, and environmental sustainability, aligned with a periodically reviewed CSR Policy and informed by stakeholder feedback. ONGC's commitment has earned multiple FY 2024–25 awards, including the Mahatma Award 2024, Asia Pacific HRM Congress Award, SHRM HR Excellence Award, NCPEDP Helen Keller Award, National Association of the Blind Sarojini Trilok Nath Award, and ICC PSE Excellence Award, recognizing its CSR impact and dedication to empowering persons with disabilities.

nodes.title: Education and Skill Training
nodes.summary: ONGC supports education and vocational training for socio-economic development. In Pauri-Garhwal, a month-long cloth bag stitching program empowered rural women, concluding with sewing machine distribution to promote sustainability and financial independence. In West Bengal, educational kits were distributed to students at a historic primary school, improving engagement. ONGC also enhances healthcare access: it donated ₹4.96 crore to Safdarjung Hospital for critical equipment, received three CSR awards in 2024, and distributed ambulances to two primary health centers in Assam, serving 25,000 residents and reducing emergency response times.

nodes.title: Community Development

It also details Social Impact Assessments, CSR initiatives by MRPL, land acquisition and rehabilitation processes, supply chain responsibility, supplier engagement and capacity building, customer centricity and product stewardship, and the way forward. nodes.title: Board Diversity and Experience

Board training covered health, safety, ethics, governance, and compliance, with 72.72% participation. Lobbying engages regulators and industry associations without political contributions. The risk management framework is multi-layered, ISO 31000:2018-aligned, with top-down and bottom-up approaches, contingency plans, and conflict-of-interest monitoring. Sustainability governance integrates ESG via the Board, CSR&ESG Committee, Risk Management Committee, Carbon Management & Sustainability Group, and HSE/CSR departments. The CSR committee is being restructured into CSR&ESGC to enhance ESG oversight, BRSR, and integrated reporting. A GRI mapping table lists disclosures and page locations.

nodes.summary: The Institute of Drilling Technology (IDT) in Dehradun advanced ONGC's drilling innovation and digital transformation. nodes.title: A. ONGC Videsh Limited
nodes.summary: ONGC Videsh Ltd, a wholly owned E&P subsidiary, holds interests in 32 oil and gas projects across 15 countries, comprising 14 producing, 4 discovered/under development, 11 exploration, and 3 pipeline projects, operating 16 itself or with partners. It has subsidiaries in Amsterdam, Singapore, Houston, and GIFT City for asset holding and treasury. FY'25 gross consolidated revenue was ₹129,946 million with PAT of ₹4,177 million. Operational highlights include production increases at CPO-5 (25% YoY), MECL (30%+ to 4,148 BOPD), GPOC (8% to ~50,400 BOPD), and SPOC (90%+ to 11,327 BOPD). Exploration successes include a first well at GPOC producing ~670 BOPD and license extensions at GPOC and SPOC, plus three exploratory wells and a new play discovery at CPO-5. Strategic acquisitions include an additional 0.615% PI in ACG and 0.737% in BTC, an addendum for NAG exploration, and an MoU for critical minerals with IRH, OIL, and KABIL.

nodes.title: B. Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL)

It has extensive marketing infrastructure, an R&D center in Bengaluru, and achieved record refining throughput of 25.27 MMT (up 13.2%), highest-ever sales volume of 49.82 MMT (up 6.4%), and record pipeline throughput of 26.90 MMT (up 9.6%). It added 1,725 retail outlets (total 23,747) and 29 LPG distributorships (total 6,378), and commenced LNG regasification at Chhara. Average GRM was US$5.74/bbl vs US$9.08. Standalone PAT was ₹73,649 million (down from ₹146,938 million) on revenue of ₹4,663,457 million (up from ₹4,616,375 million).

MRPL's refinery has complex secondary processing units and flexibility for various crude APIs. It operates an Aromatic Complex in MSEZ producing 0.905 MMTPA Para Xylene and 0.273 MMTPA Benzene, fully integrated. In FY'25, MRPL achieved record throughput of 18.044 MMT (120% capacity) vs 16.59 MMT; GRM was USD 4.45/bbl vs USD 10.36/bbl in FY'24. Standalone turnover was ₹1,092,775 million vs ₹1,052,233 million, and PAT was ₹506 million vs ₹35,959 million in FY'24.

It started ATF transportation in November 2024 and achieved its highest daily throughput in March 2025. In FY25, PMHBL reported a throughput of 3.971 MMT versus 4.05 MMT in FY24, total income of ₹2,061 million versus ₹1,857 million, and PAT of ₹830 million versus ₹963 million. Impact Assessment of CSR projects - Executive Summary
Introduction
The CSR framework introduced by the Companies Act of 2013 is a pioneering initiative, establishing India as the first nation to legislate mandatory CSR contributions. The Companies Act of 2013, Section 135, imposes a legal obligation for corporate social responsibility (CSR) on companies that satisfy certain financial criteria. ONGC has assigned the Institute of Public Enterprise, Hyderabad, with the responsibility of conducting an impact assessment for identified CSR projects. These projects spanned critical development sectors such as education, healthcare, sustainable livelihoods, culture, and sports, reflecting ONGC’s holistic approach to inclusive and sustainable development.

nodes.title: Methodology
nodes.summary: The methodology section uses mixed-method impact assessment (qualitative/quantitative, field visits, questionnaires, OECD-DAC criteria) across projects: teacher training (2,000 teachers, improved self-awareness/classroom, SDG 4/NEP 2020); handicraft artisan empowerment (income increases, reduced migration, market access); nine ALS ambulances in Assam (850+ patients annually, reduced response time, 87% survival); B.Ed college infrastructure in Arunachal Pradesh (eco-friendly, high satisfaction); sports scholarships (Asian Games medals, 70% high impact); Sanskrit promotion (1,415 trained, improved fluency); hospital wing in Mangalore (359 beds, reduced financial burden). Annexure-F covers CAG comments on ONGC financials (depreciation overstatement ₹783.66M, PPE overstatement ₹3,097.70M) with management replies. Comments summarize Board Report annexures (CAG comments, secretarial audit, MD&A, corporate governance). nodes.title: Project 2: Financial Assistance for Strategic Intervention in Handicraft Projects – Empowering Handicraft and Art and Culture
nodes.summary: The text outlines a mixed-method impact assessment using qualitative and quantitative analyses, field visits, beneficiary interactions, questionnaires, and secondary records, aligned with OECD-DAC criteria (relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, impact, sustainability). It summarizes two projects: Project 1 trained 2,000 teachers across 1,500 schools in 16 states, with post-training assessments showing improved teacher self-awareness, confidence, and classroom environments, and increased student empathy and leadership, aligning with SDG 4 and NEP 2020, though teachers struggled with extra hours. Project 2 empowered handicraft artisans, increasing incomes (e.g., Bhotiya from ₹3,000 to ₹6,000; Dhokra from ₹6,000 to ₹11,000; PwD to ₹6,000), reducing migration by 20-30%, expanding market access, and engaging youth, but noted needs for inclusive income growth, modern tools, design awareness, and a structured sales platform.

Project 3 details the provision of nine Advanced Life Saving ambulances to government medical colleges and hospitals in Assam, including equipment, improved patient service (850+ annually per ambulance), expanded rural coverage (80-100 km), reduced response time by 50%, increased survival rate to 87%, free access for rural and low-income patients, high satisfaction (>90%), and enhanced ALS availability (91%) and utility (93%). Project 4 describes financial assistance to VKVAPT for infrastructure development of a B.Ed college in Nirjuli, Arunachal Pradesh, including eco-friendly and earthquake-resistant construction, improved intake quality with waiting lists, student satisfaction with facilities (93%), learning environment (96%), safety for women (76%), laboratories (93%), library and computer lab (89%), graduate placement (81%), teacher quality improvement (96%), and notes concerns about shared compound wall security and lack of ONGC brand visibility.

Survey results show 70% reported high impact on training, 93% used funds for travel and tournament fees, 91% for essential needs like coaching and equipment, and 30% for educational requirements.

nodes.title: Project 6: Financial Support for the Promotion of Sanskrit through Training, Technology and Research for the Period 2021-23
nodes.summary: Project 6 details a Sanskrit promotion initiative (2021-23) using online multimedia tutorials, textbooks, teacher training, and spoken classes, training 1,415 participants. Survey results show improvements in pronunciation, diction, fluency (80%), reading/writing (82%), grammar/vocabulary via online modules (86%), interactive learning through digital tools (87%), and career confidence (88%). It notes the need for a comprehensive database and ONGC brand visibility. Project 7 covers ONGC-MRPL funding for a new hospital wing in Mangalore, adding 359 beds (antenatal, labour, neonatal, OT, post-op) and a human milk bank. It reports reduced financial burden (87%), high satisfaction with NICU (93%), maternal care (86%), and gynaecology services (78%). The text concludes with ONGC’s CSR commitment to inclusive development and SDGs, and mentions ONGC Videsh’s care in Colombia.

nodes.title: 1. Corporate information

nodes.summary: The text provides corporate information for Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited (ONGC), including its domicile, registered office, stock exchange listings, and the scope of its consolidated financial statements covering subsidiaries, joint ventures, and associates. nodes.title: 3. Material Group Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: This section details the Group's material accounting policies, covering consolidation principles (subsidiaries, associates, joint ventures, business combinations under common control), property, plant and equipment (including oil and gas assets, depreciation, leases), intangible assets, oil and gas accounting (acquisition, exploration, development, production, impairment), inventory valuation, revenue recognition, foreign currency translation, employee benefits (defined contribution and benefit plans), income taxes (current and deferred), borrowing costs, provisions and contingencies, financial instruments (classification, measurement, impairment, derecognition, derivatives, hedge accounting), cash and cash equivalents, investment property, earnings per share, statement of cash flows, segment reporting, and a detailed list of subsidiaries, joint ventures, and associates with ownership percentages and consolidation adjustments.

nodes.title: Consolidation procedure:
nodes.summary: The text outlines material group accounting policies, specifically principles of consolidation and business combination accounting. It covers the consolidation of subsidiaries, use of the equity method for associates and joint ventures, and control criteria. Consolidation procedures include line-by-line combination, elimination of intra-group transactions, offsetting investments, attribution of profit or loss and comprehensive income to owners and non-controlling interests, accounting for changes in ownership interests without loss of control as equity transactions, and recognition of gains or losses upon loss of control. Business combination accounting under the acquisition method is detailed, including consideration measurement, recognition of identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value with exceptions, goodwill or bargain purchase gain, non-controlling interest measurement, reassessment for bargain purchases, treatment of acquisition-related costs, step acquisitions, and provisional accounting adjustments.

nodes.title: Business Combination under Common control
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: business combinations under common control using the pooling of interests method, including asset/liability carrying amounts, policy harmonization, prior period restatement, retained earnings aggregation, and capital reserve treatment. It details non-controlling interests' initial and subsequent measurement; goodwill on consolidation, impairment testing, allocation to cash-generating units, and non-reversal of impairment; investments in associates and joint ventures using the equity method, including impairment, losses, deemed investments, and joint operation transitions; interests in joint operations, including production sharing contracts and revenue sharing contracts, with line-by-line consolidation; non-current assets held for sale measured at lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell; government grants recognition for capital and expense items, non-monetary grants, and below-market loans; and property, plant and equipment, specifically oil and gas assets, including capitalization, depletion using the unit-of-production method, and reserve estimation.

nodes.title: (ii) Other Property, Plant and Equipment
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for Property, Plant and Equipment (PPE) other than oil and gas assets, including initial measurement at cost (comprising purchase price, construction cost, directly attributable costs, decommissioning, professional fees, and capitalized borrowing costs), component accounting, and treatment of dry docking and capital improvements. It details depreciation policies: land and buildings, freehold land exceptions, useful lives review, depreciation commencement, and prospective depreciation on subsequent expenditure. It specifies depreciation methods for E&P assets (written down value, useful life ranges, overseas block license periods) and Refining & Marketing assets (straight line, useful lives, internal technical assessments for specific assets, residual values for LPG cylinders and catalysts). It covers de-recognition, gains/losses on disposal, and also lease accounting under Ind AS 116: lease identification, recognition exemptions, right-of-use asset and lease liability measurement, discount rates, and extension/termination options.

nodes.title: Asset category
nodes.summary: The text details depreciation policies: crude oil transportation using Straight Line Method per Schedule II of the Companies Act 2013, with useful lives for asset categories like buildings, plant & machinery, furniture, office equipment, vehicles, railway siding, roads, wind mills, safety lockers, and leasehold improvements. For refining & marketing, useful lives based on internal technical assessment for retail outlet plant & machinery, dispensing units, cavern structure, LPG cylinders, CNG compressors, cascades, and employee welfare assets. Specific arrangements use agreement or Schedule II, whichever lower. Residual values: LPG cylinders 25%, noble metal catalysts 90%. Overhaul and repair costs for planned shutdowns are capitalized and depreciated; catalysts with life >1 year capitalized and depreciated over guaranteed life. Leasehold land immovable assets depreciated over Schedule II or lease period. Lease liabilities and right-of-use assets: lease identification at inception, control assessment, and exemption for intangible asset leases.

nodes.title: Group as a lessee
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Group's lease accounting as a lessee under Ind AS 116. It covers initial recognition of ROU assets and lease liabilities, exemptions for short-term and low-value leases, treatment of extension/termination options, initial and subsequent measurement including discount rates and depreciation, remeasurement upon reassessment, and accounting for unincorporated joint operations based on primary responsibility. It also addresses interest cost expensing or capitalization, separation of lease and non-lease components with a practical expedient for subsidiary HPCL, and allocation of consideration based on stand-alone prices.

nodes.title: Group as Lessor:
nodes.summary: The text covers lessor accounting for leases, classifying finance leases that transfer substantially all risks and rewards and operating leases with straight-line rental income recognition. It details intangible assets: recognition at cost net of amortization/impairment, non-capitalization of internally generated intangibles except development costs under specific conditions, treatment of research and development expenditure, amortization over useful lives or agreement periods, classification of constructed assets with preferential use rights and committed-output assets, annual impairment testing for indefinite-lived assets like right of way, derecognition gains/losses, recognition of technical know-how/license fees, estimated useful lives for software, technical know-how, licenses, and wind mill rights, and capitalization and subsequent treatment of exploratory well costs.

nodes.title: Intangible Oil & Gas Assets in progress
nodes.summary: The text details accounting policies for oil and gas assets: capitalization of survey costs as intangible assets until transfer; impairment testing for tangible, intangible, and right-of-use assets at each reporting period, including CGU recoverable amount estimation, annual testing for indefinite-life intangibles, and reversal of impairment losses. It covers impairment of acquisition costs for participating rights, allocation to CGUs, and non-reversal. Carried interest arrangements are recognized as financial or other assets, with provisions for exploration-stage projects and cost-based carrying for development-stage projects. Exploration and evaluation costs are expensed pre-acquisition, while acquisition costs are capitalized and transferred upon production readiness, with write-off on abandonment. Production costs include pre- and post-well head expenses.

nodes.title: Impairment of Acquisition cost relating to participating rights
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for impairment reversal of acquisition costs, allocation to cash-generating units (CGUs), and disposal treatment; carried interest arrangements, recognition as financial or other assets, and provisions for exploration and development stages; exploration and evaluation costs including pre-acquisition, acquisition, survey, development wells, and production costs; impairment of acquisition costs for participating rights; side-tracking cost treatment for exploratory, development, and producing wells; decommissioning cost recognition, measurement, and joint operations; and inventory valuation for raw materials, stock in process, and finished goods.

nodes.title: Exploration and Production Operation (E&P)
nodes.summary:
Exploration and Production Operation (E&P)
Finished goods (other than Sulphur and carbon credits) including inventories in pipelines/ tanks are valued at cost or net realisable value whichever is lower. Cost of finished goods is determined on absorption costing method.
Crude oil in semi-finished condition at Group Gathering Stations (GGS) is valued at cost on absorption costing method or net realisable value whichever is lower except where the same is parked as per the provision of relevant gas sale agreement (GSA).
Crude oil in unfinished condition in flow lines up to GGS/ platform is not valued as the same is not measurable. Natural Gas is not valued as it is not stored.
Sulphur (being residual in nature) and carbon credits are valued at net realisable value.
Cost of finished goods and semi-finished goods are determined on weighted average basis.

nodes.title: Refining & Petrochemicals
nodes.summary: The text details valuation methods for refining and petrochemicals: finished goods excluding lubricants and petrochemicals are valued at lower of FIFO cost (raw material, conversion, excise duty) or net realisable value; lubricants and petrochemical finished/semi-finished products at lower of weighted average cost or net realisable value. Stock in trade and empty packages use weighted average cost; semi-finished goods cost includes raw material and proportionate conversion. Customs duty on bonded warehouse raw materials/finished goods is provided unless liability transfers to consignee; excise duty on finished stocks at manufacturing locations is based on assessable value and applicable duty. Net realisable value uses final selling prices to oil marketing companies and depot prices, with sales proportions determined by subsequent location and product-wise sales.

nodes.title: (c) Store & Spares
nodes.summary: The text covers inventory valuation for stores and spares, including weighted average cost or net realisable value, provisions for obsolete items, and treatment of surplus and in-transit items. nodes.title: Foreign Currency Translation and Employee Benefits Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: The text details accounting policies for foreign currency transactions and employee benefits. It covers translation of monetary and non-monetary items, recognition of exchange differences, treatment of long-term foreign currency monetary items, disposal of foreign operations, goodwill and fair value adjustments, and translation to presentation currency. Employee benefits section defines short-term benefits, and defined contribution plans including provident fund, pension, and social security, recognized at undiscounted amounts paid to separate trusts.

nodes.title: Defined benefit plans
nodes.summary: The text details accounting policies for defined benefit plans (provident fund, gratuity, post-retirement medical, resettlement, felicitation, terminal benefits) using projected unit credit method, including net interest and remeasurements. It covers other long-term benefits (leave encashment, compensated absences), termination benefits, and contributions to fund trusts and LIC. It also addresses administrative expenses allocation, insurance claims recognition, and income taxes: current tax based on taxable profit, and deferred tax using balance sheet method with recognition, measurement, review, offsetting, and presentation principles, including exceptions for initial recognition and investments in subsidiaries.

nodes.title: Employee Benefits, Administrative Expenses, Insurance Claims, and Income Taxes
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting policies for retirement benefits (net interest, remeasurement, contributions to trusts, surplus limitation, termination benefits), other long-term employee benefits (leave encashment and compensated absences using projected unit credit method, remeasurements in profit and loss, contributions to LIC), administrative expenses (direct allocation and general charges), insurance claims (recognized when reliably measurable and virtually certain), and income taxes (current tax based on taxable profit and enacted rates, deferred tax using balance sheet method with recognition criteria, measurement, offsetting, and presentation).

nodes.title: Deferred tax
nodes.summary: This text covers accounting policies: net interest on defined benefit liabilities; remeasurements in OCI; contributions to fund trusts; surplus limitation; other long-term benefits like leave encashment using projected unit credit; termination benefits; administrative expenses allocation; insurance claims recognition; income taxes including current and deferred tax, MAT, and exceptions; borrowing costs capitalization and suspension; rig days cost; provisions, contingent liabilities and assets; and financial instruments including initial recognition, transaction costs, and classification as debt or equity.

nodes.title: (i) Classification as debt or equity instruments
nodes.summary: The text covers classification of debt and equity instruments based on contractual substance, and accounting for compound financial instruments, including separate liability and equity components, fair value estimation, conversion option treatment, and transaction cost allocation. It also details financial assets: initial recognition at fair value (except trade receivables at transaction price), classification into amortized cost, FVTOCI, or FVTPL based on business model and cash flow characteristics, subsequent measurement, treatment of equity investments, and impairment using the expected credit loss model under Ind AS 109.

nodes.title: Compound Financial Instruments and Classification of Financial Assets
key_items: • Financial Assets at Fair value through OCI (FVTOCI)
• Financial Assets at Fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL)
nodes.summary: The text covers compound financial instruments and financial assets. For compound instruments, it details separate classification of liability and equity components based on contractual substance, initial measurement of the liability component at fair value using market interest rate, equity component as residual, treatment upon conversion or maturity, and allocation of transaction costs. For financial assets, it covers initial recognition at fair value (except trade receivables at transaction price) and treatment of transaction costs. Classification and subsequent measurement are based on business model and contractual cash flow characteristics: amortized cost (held to collect solely principal and interest, using effective interest method), FVTOCI (held to collect and sell, with fair value movements in OCI, interest/impairment/FX in P&L, and recycling on derecognition), FVTPL (default category, transaction costs expensed), and investments in equity instruments (fair value, trading at FVTPL, others irrevocably elected as FVTOCI or FVTPL; FVTPL changes in P&L; FVTOCI changes in OCI excluding dividends in P&L, no recycling, but transfer within equity on disposal).

nodes.title: (ii) Impairment of financial assets
nodes.summary: This text outlines the Group's accounting policies under Ind AS 109 for financial instruments. It covers impairment of financial assets using the expected credit loss (ECL) model, distinguishing between the simplified approach for trade receivables (lifetime ECL) and the general approach for other financial assets (12-month ECL unless credit risk increases significantly, then lifetime ECL), including consideration of forward-looking information. It also details derecognition of financial assets. For financial liabilities, it covers initial recognition at fair value, subsequent measurement at amortized cost, derecognition, and specific treatment of financial guarantee contracts. Finally, it addresses derivative financial instruments, including initial recognition, subsequent fair value measurement, hedge accounting (cash flow hedges), and embedded derivatives.

nodes.title: Impairment, Derecognition, Financial Liabilities, Guarantees, and Derivatives
nodes.summary: The page covers impairment of financial assets: trade receivables use lifetime expected credit losses (ECL) under the simplified approach; other financial assets like Cash Call receivables follow the general approach, recognizing 12-month ECL unless credit risk increases significantly, then lifetime ECL, with reversion if credit quality improves. It details derecognition of financial assets when rights expire or transfer qualifies, with gains/losses in profit or loss. Financial liabilities are initially at fair value, subsequently at amortized cost, and derecognized when obligations discharge. Financial guarantee contracts are initially at fair value, subsequently at the higher of loss allowance or initially recognized amount less cumulative income. Derivative financial instruments are initially at fair value, remeasured at fair value through profit or loss unless designated as hedging instruments, and embedded derivatives are separated under certain conditions.

nodes.title: Derivatives Contracts designated as hedging instruments
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: hedge accounting for derivatives designated as hedging instruments, including designation, documentation, fair value recognition, cash flow hedge treatment (effective portion in OCI, ineffective in P&L, reclassification, discontinuation), and non-occurrence of forecasted transactions; derivatives not designated as hedging instruments at fair value through P&L; embedded derivatives separation criteria; offsetting of financial instruments; cash and cash equivalents definition; investment property initial and subsequent measurement, depreciation, and derecognition; earnings per share (basic and diluted); statement of cash flows using indirect method; and segment reporting based on CODM, including segment revenue, expenses, and unallocated items.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies: Derivatives, Financial Instruments, Cash, Property, EPS, Cash Flows

Derivatives not designated as hedges are at fair value through P&L; embedded derivatives are separated unless closely related. Offsetting of financial instruments requires legal right and intent for net settlement. Cash equivalents are highly liquid instruments with maturities up to three months. nodes.title: Determination of cash generating unit (CGU)
nodes.summary:
Determination of cash generating unit (CGU)
The Group is engaged mainly in the business of oil and gas exploration and production in Onshore and Offshore. In case of onshore assets, the fields are using common production/ transportation facilities and are sufficiently economically interdependent to constitute a single cash generating unit (CGU). Accordingly, impairment test of all onshore fields in India is performed in aggregate of all those fields at the Asset Level. In case of Offshore Assets, a field is generally considered as CGU except for fields which are developed as a Cluster or group of Clusters, for which common facilities are used, in which case the impairment testing is performedin aggregate for all the fields included in the cluster or group of Clusters.

nodes.title: (d) Impairment of assets
nodes.summary: This text details the methodology for assessing impairment of Cash Generating Units (CGUs), involving management estimates of uncertain factors like future prices, inflation, discount rates, and production profiles for oil, gas, and value-added products. It explains cash flow estimation for Oil & Gas assets using best estimates of prices, production, and reserves, with present values determined via pre-tax discount rates in US$. For natural gas, future prices are based on Government of India notifications and discounted accordingly. For subsidiary ONGC Videsh Ltd., discount rates reflect market assessments and risks, with crude oil prices based on Brent forward prices from Bloomberg or third parties, and gas prices from agreements or forecasts. Production profiles consider all contractually possible extensions. Discount rates use a cost of capital model. Value in use is determined via a multi-stage approach using Proved Developed Reserves, or Proved and Probable (2P) reserves when development is ongoing and carrying value may not be recoverable from proved developed reserves alone, including full expected evaluation/development costs. Discount rates are re-assessed annually.

nodes.title: (e) Estimation of reserves
nodes.summary: The text covers estimation of oil and gas reserves, including management's use of the Reserves Estimation Committee (REC) following PRMS (2018) definitions for Proved, Developed, and Undeveloped Reserves. It details volumetric and performance estimation methods, annual revision triggers from exploration, appraisal, and technology changes, and the inherent imprecision and auditing limitations of reserves estimates, with third-party audits. It also addresses defined benefit obligations (DBO) assumptions, litigation provisions and judgment, and impairment of financial assets using the ECL model under Ind AS 109, including rating-based and general approaches with forward-looking macroeconomic indicators.

nodes.title: Reserves Estimation, Auditing, DBO and Litigation Provisions
nodes.summary: The page covers reserve estimation and auditing, including revisions from technology, classification, and contractual changes, and SPE standards highlighting inherent imprecision and uncertainty in reserves data. It notes third-party due diligence and periodic audits by reputed consultants. It also addresses the defined benefit obligation (DBO), which relies on critical assumptions such as inflation, medical cost trends, mortality, discount rate, and salary increases, with variations significantly impacting DBO and expenses. Finally, it discusses litigations, noting uncertain outcomes, provisions when payment is probable and estimable, significant judgment in assessing unfavorable outcomes and losses, and periodic reviews with revisions for changes in facts and circumstances.

nodes.title: Impairment of Financial Assets

Impairment of Financial Assets
In accordance with Ind AS 109 - Financial Instruments, the Company applies ECL model for measurement and recognition of impairment loss on the trade receivables and other financial assets. For trade receivables, the Company follows rating-based approach to compute default rates based on Credit ratings of the borrowers and forward-looking estimates are incorporated using relevant macroeconomic indicator (GDP growth rate).
For other financial assets, the Company applies general approach for recognition of impairment losses wherein the Company uses judgment in considering the probability of default upon initial recognition and whether there has been a significant increase in credit risk on an ongoing basis throughout each reporting period.

Section 52 covers financial instruments disclosure.

nodes.title: 52.1 Capital Management
nodes.summary: This text covers capital management objectives, including safeguarding going concern status and maintaining optimal capital structure. It details financial framework, capital structure components (net debt and total equity), and regular reviews by financial management committees. It presents gearing ratio calculations with debt, cash balances, net debt, total equity, and net debt to equity ratio. It categorizes financial instruments into FVTPL, amortised cost, and FVTOCI for assets and liabilities. Finally, it outlines financial risk management objectives, including credit, liquidity, and market risks, and describes subsidiary-specific approaches (OVL, HPCL, PMHBL, MRPL, OPaL, OGL) involving derivatives, ERM frameworks, and risk committees.

nodes.title: Measured at amortised cost
nodes.summary: The text presents consolidated financial statements with two years of comparative figures. It categorizes financial assets measured at amortized cost, including trade receivables, cash equivalents, other bank balances, site restoration fund deposits, loans, and other financial assets, and at FVTOCI, including equity investments. Financial liabilities include derivative liabilities at FVTPL and liabilities at amortized cost such as short-term and long-term borrowings, trade payables, other financial liabilities (compulsory convertible debentures, financial guarantee contracts, others), and lease liabilities. Numeric values are provided for each line item across both periods.

nodes.title: 52.3 Financial risk management objectives
nodes.summary: The text outlines financial risk management objectives and credit risk management for a Group and its subsidiaries. It covers monitoring credit, liquidity, and market risks (including currency and price risks) through exposure analysis. For the Company, it details comfortable liquidity, bank credit lines, a ₹100,000 million commercial paper limit, and continuous cash flow review. For subsidiaries OVL, HPCL, PMHBL, MRPL, OPaL, and OGL, it describes risk mitigation via derivatives, an Enterprise Risk Management framework, risk committee oversight, technology-enabled risk reporting, and focus on minimizing adverse financial effects. Credit risk management covers counterparty limits, high-rated investments, negligible credit risk from public sector customers, financial guarantee exposure of ₹437,210.35 million, expected credit loss modeling, and loss allowance movement.

nodes.title: Credit Risk Management for Company and Subsidiary OVL
nodes.summary: The page covers credit risk management, including sources of credit risk, use of forward-looking information, counterparty limits, investment and deposit policies, and low credit risk from major public sector customers. It details the Company's exposure to financial guarantees for subsidiaries and joint ventures, the expected credit loss model under Ind AS 109, and a table showing movement in loss allowance for various financial assets. It also notes credit exposure limits for other counterparties and high-rated bank policies, repeating similar points for subsidiary OVL.

nodes.title: In respect of subsidiary MRPL,
nodes.summary: The text details credit risk management across subsidiaries MRPL, PMHBL, HPCL, OPaL, and OGL. MRPL's major customers are high-rated OMCs/IOCs/NOCs with negligible risk. PMHBL's trade receivables are from 4 CPSE customers with long-term relationships; expected credit losses are immaterial, but provisions are made for old doubtful debts. HPCL manages credit risk through approvals, limits, and monitoring; maximum exposure is carrying amount. OPaL considers forward-looking information like credit ratings and macro-economic data. OGL's significant concentration is trade receivables; credit quality is assessed, and counterparty limits are set. HPCL's trade receivables use an allowance matrix with loss rates by ageing: 0-90 days (0.10%), 91-360 days (11.57%), and >360 days (64.55%), with corresponding gross amounts and allowances for 2025 and 2024.

nodes.title: Credit Risk Disclosures for Subsidiaries and Trade Receivables
key_items: Trade receivables: In respect of HPCL,
nodes.summary: The page presents credit risk disclosures for subsidiaries PMHBL, HPCL, OPaL, and OGL, and trade receivables for HPCL. For PMHBL, maximum exposure is from trade receivables (Nil both years), mostly from 4 CPSE customers, with expected credit loss model applied but negligible bad debts; security includes deposits and letters of credit. HPCL covers credit risk from receivables and investments, managed via approvals, limits, and monitoring, with exposure limited to carrying amounts. OPaL discusses credit risk from cash, bank deposits, and receivables, using forward-looking information like credit ratings and macro-economic data. OGL addresses trade receivables concentration, counterparty limits, and high-rated bank deposits. HPCL trade receivables section details individual and grouped impairment assessment using an allowance matrix, with a table showing exposure and loss allowance for 2025 and 2024.

nodes.title: Gross carrying amount
nodes.summary: The text details trade receivables aging with gross carrying amounts, loss rates, and loss allowance movements for trade receivables and PMUY loans. It describes write-offs due to customer defaults, cash and cash equivalents holdings, and investment policies for surplus funds, forex/interest rate derivatives, and debt securities. It also covers OPaL's subsidiary impairment assessment, credit risk management for receivables, and liquidity risk management including contractual maturity analysis of financial liabilities.

nodes.title: Credit Risk and Cash Management Disclosures
nodes.summary: The page details loss allowance movements for trade receivables and PMUY loans for 2023-2025, including recognized, reversed, and written-off amounts due to customer defaults. It covers cash and cash equivalents held with scheduled banks and investments in low-risk instruments like T-bills, TREPS, CROMS, and mutual funds. Derivative exposures are with investment-grade banks and reputable OTC counterparties, with monitored limits. Debt securities are sovereign, carrying no credit risk. For subsidiary OPaL, impairment assessment for receivables from plastic and petrochemical companies is described, including credit terms (T+2/T+14 days), interest on delays, advance/LC-based sales, and collateral-backed channel partner sales, concluding no significant credit risk concentration.

nodes.title: 52.5 Liquidity risk management
nodes.summary: The text addresses liquidity risk management, covering the Group's approach to maintaining sufficient cash, cash equivalents, and committed credit facilities; monitoring rolling forecasts and cash flows; projecting cash flows by matching maturity profiles and monitoring liquidity ratios. It presents tables detailing contractual maturity (less than 1 month) of financial liabilities—borrowings, trade payables, other financial liabilities, intergroup eliminations, and financial guarantee obligations—for FY 2024-25 and FY 2023-24, including interest and principal cash flows based on earliest repayment dates. A footnote defines financial guarantee obligation exposure. It also notes that obligations will be met from operating cash flows and maturing financial assets, with access to committed credit facilities.

nodes.title: In respect of the Company,
nodes.summary: The text covers liquidity and financing arrangements for the Company and its subsidiaries. For the Company, it details the US$2 billion EMTN program set up in 2019 and updated in 2021, the issuance of NCDs aggregating ₹41,400 million in FY2020-21, access to committed credit facilities including unsecured bank overdraft, cash credit limits, short-term loan facilities, and commercial paper limits, with amounts used and unused. For subsidiary MRPL, it describes secured bank overdraft facility with unused amounts. For subsidiary OVL, it provides a liquidity analysis of derivative financial instruments, specifically foreign exchange forward contracts. For subsidiary PMHBL, it states no outstanding bank borrowings and sufficient working capital. For subsidiary HPCL, it outlines financing arrangements, including diversified funding sources and credit rating access. For subsidiary OPaL, it describes liquidity risk management through cash, committed credit facilities, and monitoring of forecasts and ratios.

nodes.title: Subsidiary Derivative Liquidity and Liquidity Risk Disclosures
nodes.summary: The page presents liquidity analysis for subsidiary OVL's derivative financial instruments, showing undiscounted contractual net cash inflows and outflows for foreign exchange forward contracts settling on a gross basis, with tables for March 31, 2025, and March 31, 2024, across maturity buckets (less than 3 months, 3–6 months, 6 months–1 year, more than 1 year) and carrying amounts. It then covers subsidiary PMHBL, stating its principal liquidity sources are cash, cash equivalents, and operating cash flow, with no outstanding bank borrowings, and that working capital is sufficient, so no liquidity risk is perceived. The page ends with a heading for subsidiary HPCL but provides no content.

nodes.title: Financing Arrangement
nodes.summary: The text covers the Group's financing arrangements, including bank lines, borrowing limits, credit ratings, and diversified funding sources across maturities and currencies. It lists financing products such as syndicated loans, bonds, term loans, TREPS, CROMS, commercial paper, debentures, and buyer's credit. For Subsidiary OPaL, it details liquidity risk management through cash reserves, credit facilities, and cash flow forecasting, and provides undrawn borrowing facilities. Market risk is discussed for the Group and subsidiaries, focusing on commodity price, foreign currency, and interest rate risks, including crude oil exposure and Ukraine-Russia conflict assessment. Foreign currency risk management is outlined for the Company, covering hedging policies, FRMC oversight, and hedging instruments.

nodes.title: Liquidity, Financing Arrangements, and Market Risk Disclosures
nodes.summary: The page covers liquidity risk management through reserves, cash flow monitoring, and maturity matching, and lists undrawn borrowing facilities (₹8,207.09 million at March 31, 2025; ₹12,251.59 million at March 31, 2024). It defines market risk and its components: commodity price, foreign currency, and interest rate risk. For the Company, it discusses exposure to international crude oil and gas prices, assesses the Ukraine-Russia conflict's impact as insignificant, and notes ongoing macro analysis. For subsidiary OVL, it covers crude oil price risk and derivative use for foreign currency, with no derivatives outstanding at March 31, 2025. For subsidiary PMHBL, it notes small international exposure and potentially insignificant exchange rate impact.

nodes.title: 52.7 Foreign currency risk management
nodes.summary: The text covers foreign currency risk management for the company and its subsidiaries. It details the company's exposure to US$ due to crude oil sales, risk mitigation through natural hedging and a Foreign Exchange and Interest Risk Management Policy, overseen by a Forex Risk Management Committee. Hedging instruments include forwards and options, with decisions triggered if net exposure exceeds US$500 million, though no hedging occurred this year. For subsidiaries HPCL, MRPL, OVL, and OPaL, their specific currency risks and management approaches are outlined. The text also presents foreign currency denominated monetary assets and liabilities as of March 31, 2025 and 2024, and a foreign currency sensitivity analysis showing the impact of +/-5% exchange rate changes on profit or loss for the company and MRPL, as well as sensitivity of revenue to exchange rate changes.

nodes.title: Liabilities:
nodes.summary: The text details foreign currency risk exposure for the Group and its subsidiaries HPCL, MRPL, OVL, and OPaL, covering sources such as foreign currency loans, imports, crude oil purchases, exports, and borrowings. It describes the Forex Risk Management Cell's oversight, use of derivative contracts for mitigation (not trading/speculation), and functional currency for OVL. It presents carrying amounts of foreign currency monetary assets and liabilities as of March 31, 2025, and 2024, in USD, GBP, EURO, AED, JPY, RUB, and others. Foreign currency sensitivity analysis for the Company and MRPL is provided, showing +/-5% exchange rate impacts on profit or loss and revenue sensitivity to +/-1 INR/USD change, with a note on representativeness.

nodes.title: Payables:
nodes.summary: The text presents foreign currency risk sensitivity analyses for the Group and its subsidiaries (OVL, HPCL, OPaL) under consolidated financial statements. It details impacts on profit or loss from ±5% USD-INR and EUR-INR fluctuations on borrowings, receivables, and payables for years ended March 31, 2024, and 2025, including specific figures. It notes management's caveat on sensitivity representativeness, describes HPCL's 1% USD/INR movement analysis, and OPaL's USD and EURO exposures. It also covers forward foreign exchange contracts (none for the Company; OVL uses them) and introduces interest rate risk management, including a sensitivity analysis for the Company's benchmarked borrowings.

nodes.title: Financial liabilities
nodes.summary: The text presents foreign currency and interest rate risk disclosures from consolidated financial statements. It details US$ sensitivity at year-end for receivables and payables for FY2025 and FY2024, including a 5% weakening/strengthening impact. For subsidiary OVL, it notes exposure to foreign currency borrowings (outstanding `2,346.97 million as of March 31, 2025) and provides a 5% USD-INR sensitivity analysis on profit or loss. For subsidiary HPCL, it shows a 1% USD/INR movement sensitivity on open forex exposure. For subsidiary OPaL, it provides 5% USD and EURO sensitivity for financial assets and liabilities. It also covers forward foreign exchange contracts: the Company had none, while OVL uses them to hedge specific payments/receipts. Finally, it discusses interest rate risk management, including fixed and floating rate borrowings, interest rate sensitivity analysis, short-term bank deposits with no significant risk, and average interest earned (7.85% vs. 7.67% prior year), noting fixed rate instruments at amortized cost are not subject to interest rate risk.

nodes.title: Cash flow sensitivity analysis for variable-rate instruments
nodes.summary: The text presents cash flow sensitivity analyses for variable-rate instruments, showing the impact of a ±50 basis point change in interest rates. It details the sensitivity of finance cost for 2023-24 and 2024-25, with impacts of ±47.37 million and ±32.13 million, respectively. For subsidiary MRPL, a 50 basis point change would affect profit by ±232.16 million for FY2025 and ±260.32 million for FY2024. For subsidiary OVL, the analysis covers non-derivative instruments, listing specific US dollar facilities (e.g., $800 million, $500 million, $600 million, $100 million, $420 million, $550 million, $450 million) and their impacts on profit or loss for FY2025 and FY2024, with corresponding increases and decreases in interest rates.

nodes.title: Particulars
nodes.summary: The text details interest rate risk management, covering exposure to MCLR, Treasury Bills, debt market, and RBI Repo; investment of surplus funds in short-term bank deposits and mutual funds with average interest earned; fixed-rate instruments at amortized cost not subject to interest rate risk; cash flow sensitivity analysis for variable-rate instruments showing impact on finance cost; and subsidiary-specific analyses for MRPL, OVL, OPaL, OGL, and HPCL, including sensitivity of profit to 50 basis point changes, interest rate swap contracts, interest rate risk exposure with carrying amounts of fixed and variable rate instruments, and cash flow sensitivity to 25 basis point changes.

nodes.title: Interest Rate Risk Disclosures for Subsidiaries and Group
nodes.summary: The text presents interest rate risk disclosures for subsidiary OPaL, OGL, and HPCL, including sensitivity analyses. For OPaL, a 50 basis point change would affect profit by ₹1134.47 million (2025) and ₹1295.89 million (2024) due to variable rate borrowings. OGL describes interest rate risk from floating rate long-term debt, management by fixing initial rates, and a sensitivity of ±₹28.25 million on profit before tax. Interest rate swap contracts are noted: the Company (E&P business) entered none, while HPCL uses floating-to-fixed swaps to manage cash flow risk on USD syndicated loans, with no speculative trading. Fixed-rate borrowings are carried at amortized cost and not affected. HPCL's interest rate exposure shows carrying amounts of fixed-rate instruments (financial assets ₹430,889.03 million, liabilities ₹353,787.59 million as of 31.03.2025) and variable-rate instruments (assets ₹233,399.77 million, liabilities ₹274,343.61 million). Cash flow sensitivity for variable-rate instruments indicates a 25 basis point change would impact profit or loss by ±₹516.34 million (2025) and ±₹530.94 million (2024).

nodes.summary: The text covers commodity risk management for HPCL, including exposure to crude oil and petroleum price fluctuations, monitoring via an Oil Price Risk Management Committee, and derivative contracts in the OTC market. It provides quantitative data on outstanding commodity derivative contracts (swaps) and sensitivity analysis showing the impact of a 10% price change on profit before tax for 2025 and 2024. It details hedge accounting under Ind AS 109 for commodity and foreign exchange derivatives, including mark-to-market adjustments in Other Comprehensive Income, a 1:1 hedge ratio, and sources of hedge effectiveness and ineffectiveness. Disclosures on cash flow hedges are also mentioned.

nodes.title: Commodity Risk, Derivatives, Hedging and Hedge Effectiveness
nodes.summary: The page covers commodity risk from crude oil and petroleum price fluctuations for subsidiary HPCL, monitored via an Oil Price Risk Management Policy and OPRMC. It includes quantitative break-up of outstanding commodity derivative contracts (Crude/Product Swaps) as of 31.03.2025 and 31.03.2024, and sensitivity analysis showing the effect on profit before tax for a 10% price change. It details derivative contracts used for hedging commodity price risk and currency risk, application of hedge accounting under Ind AS 109, and mark-to-market amounts in Other Comprehensive Income. Hedge effectiveness is addressed through a 1:1 hedge ratio, economic relationship between hedged items and instruments, and sources of hedge ineffectiveness for commodity and foreign currency risk.

nodes.title: Disclosures of effects of Cash Flow Hedge Accounting:
nodes.summary: The text covers disclosures on Cash Flow Hedge Accounting effects, including prospective application for highly probable forecast transactions and foreign exchange forwards. It details derivative contracts held as of March 31, 2025 and 2024, with maturities and nominal amounts for commodity forwards and foreign exchange forwards for loans and crude/product liabilities. It also presents the impact of hedging instruments on the balance sheet, showing carrying amounts and line items, and the impact of cash flow hedges on the statement of Profit and Loss and Other Comprehensive Income.

nodes.title: Derivative Contracts and Hedging Impacts on Financial Statements
nodes.summary: The page presents the company's derivative contracts, including commodity forward contracts and foreign exchange forward contracts for loans and crude/product liabilities. It details maturities by month ranges (less than 1, 1-3, 3-6, 6-12, more than 12 months) for March 31, 2025, and March 31, 2024, showing nominal volumes and amounts. It also covers the impact of hedging instruments on the balance sheet, specifying nominal and carrying amounts across line items for commodity and foreign currency forward contracts for both years. Additionally, it addresses the impact of cash flow hedges on the statement of profit and loss and other comprehensive income.

nodes.title: Foreign Exchange Forward Contracts - Crude/product liabilities
nodes.summary: The text covers derivative contracts (commodity and foreign exchange forwards) with maturities and nominal amounts as of March 31, 2025 and 2024, including hedging impact on the balance sheet and cash flow hedge effects in P&L and OCI. It details price risks from equity investments and crude oil/natural gas price changes, with sensitivity analyses for the company and subsidiaries OVL and HPCL. Fair value measurement is discussed, including the three-level hierarchy, valuation techniques for financial assets and liabilities, and a table of fair values by category as of both dates.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurement of Financial Assets and Liabilities
key_items: 53.2.1 Fair value of the Group’s financial assets that are measured at fair value on a recurring basis
nodes.summary: The page covers fair value measurement under note 53.2, explaining how the Group determines fair values of financial assets and liabilities. It details recurring fair value measurement of financial assets, the three-level fair value hierarchy (Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs, Level 3 unobservable inputs), and notes no changes in Level 3 methodology, no material Level 3 instruments, and no transfers between levels for 2025 and 2024. A table presents fair values as at March 31, 2025 and 2024 for employee loans measured at amortized cost (Level 2, discounted cash flows), FVTOCI investments in quoted and unquoted equity instruments, and FVTPL investments in unquoted equity instruments, along with valuation techniques and key inputs.

nodes.title: Financial Liabilities: Measured at amortized cost:
nodes.summary: The text covers financial liabilities measured at amortized cost, including financial guarantees and lease liabilities with values, and fair value hierarchy levels (1, 2, 3) with valuation techniques like quoted prices, discounted cash flow, and interest rate differential models. It details security deposits, compulsory convertible debentures, and fair value measurements for mutual funds, other investments, and derivative liabilities, with specific values for March 31, 2025, and 2024. It includes a table of financial assets and liabilities (investments, loans, borrowings, derivatives) classified by level, and explains judgments and estimates in determining fair value under Indian Accounting Standards, noting omissions where carrying amount approximates fair value.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurement of Financial Assets and Liabilities
key_items: As at March As at March 31, 2025 31, 2024
nodes.summary: The page presents fair value disclosures for subsidiary OVL and HPCL, covering financial assets and liabilities measured at fair value. It includes tables showing fair values of investments, mutual funds, other investments, and derivative liabilities as at March 31, 2025, and 2024. Valuation techniques and inputs are explained, including Level 1 NAV, Level 2 mark-to-market reports, and Level 3 unobservable inputs. A fair value hierarchy table classifies financial assets (equity, preference shares, debt instruments, loans, derivatives) and financial liabilities (bonds, debentures, loans, derivatives) into Level 1, 2, and 3, with amounts for both years. The section also describes judgements, estimates, and Indian Accounting Standard classifications.

nodes.title: Level 3
nodes.summary: The text details fair value measurement of financial assets and liabilities across subsidiaries OVL, HPCL, MRPL, and OGL. It includes tables showing fair values of mutual funds, other investments, and derivative liabilities for OVL; HPCL's fair value hierarchy levels (1-3) with valuation techniques, inputs, and carrying amounts for investments, loans, derivatives, and borrowings as of March 31, 2025 and 2024; valuation techniques for derivatives (forward contracts, commodities, interest rate swaps) and amortized cost items; MRPL's classification of financial liabilities at amortized cost as Level II; and OGL's assessment that carrying amounts approximate fair values for short-term instruments, with methods for amortized cost assets and a table comparing carrying and fair values of financial assets and liabilities.

nodes.title: Fair Value Valuation Techniques and Carrying Values

nodes.summary: Imperial Energy operations continue per Business Plan despite crude price discounts. Five subsidiaries (IECL, IENL, RHL, BHL, SAIL) were dissolved without liquidation via merger into Imperial Energy, approved by Cyprus Court Decree on 16 April 2024, effective 22 April 2024, with certificate issued 24 May 2024; all assets and liabilities were transferred, with no group reporting impact. Management monitors geopolitical situations and sanctions. Other current assets include ₹392.26 million from underlifted oil (expected to settle in kind), and other current liabilities include ₹3.44 million from overlifted oil. The Vietnam Block 06.1 PSC was extended for 16 years from 19 May 2023, with possible two-year further extension; production continues with regulator support and compensation via side agreement; exploration drilling awaits government approval, with a future minimum work program commitment of ₹856.80 million (OVL share ₹385.56 million). OVL has not opted for lower tax rate under Section 115BAA. The company acquired an additional 0.615% PI in ACG Project from Equinor for adjusted consideration of ₹4,787.02 million, completed on 29 November 2024; fair value of net assets acquired was ₹4,901.13 million, resulting in capital reserve of ₹114.11 million, consolidated line by line under Ind AS 103.
